name: Sculpting stick

card.summary: A cream or balm stick used to contour the face, adding shadow under cheekbones and jaw and highlight on top to make bone structure look more defined.

quick.overview:
A sculpting or contour stick is a makeup product in stick form, usually a cream or balm, used to add shadow and highlight to the face. Placed under the cheekbones, along the jaw, at the temples or at the sides of the nose, it creates the look of stronger structure.

The effect is cosmetic and lasts while worn. It is one of the more approachable contouring tools because it can be applied directly and blended with fingers, a sponge or a brush.
quick.how: People swipe a shade one to two tones darker than their skin where they want shadow, often a little higher on the cheek than feels natural, and blend the edges until the line disappears. A lighter shade or a cream blush can go on the high points. Many sticks double as bronzer or eyeshadow. Cream contour usually goes on over foundation and before powder, and it is removed with regular makeup remover.
quick.risks: Cream sticks can feel heavy on oily or acne-prone skin and may clog pores for some people. Ingredients can cause allergic or irritant reactions in sensitive skin, and sharing sticks can spread bacteria. Because a stick is not applied across the whole face, makeup brands note it does not replace sunscreen.

lead: A sculpting stick, also called a contour stick, is a solid cream or balm makeup product for shaping the face with shadow and light. Because it comes as a stick, it is portable and can be swiped directly onto the skin before blending [1][2].

Contouring uses a shade one or two tones darker than the skin on the cheek hollows, sides of the nose and temples to suggest shadow, with lighter tones on prominent areas to bring them forward [3]. People use it to emphasise cheekbones, jawline or nose shape for photos and events, and sticks are favoured for being easy to blend and often serving several purposes in one product [1][2].
The technique has a long history in theatre and film makeup, and stick formats became a social-media favourite in the 2020s [3][1].

chain: Apply a darker shade under cheekbones or along the jaw
Add a lighter shade or blush on high points
Blend for a more defined face while worn
angle.text: A sculpting stick adds the look of definition to the face by painting in shadow and highlight. The effect is immediate and lasts until the makeup is removed.

paras: Sticks come in contour shades (cool or neutral brown), highlight shades and sometimes blush or bronzer tones, and some products pair a contour shade at one end with a highlighter at the other. Wikipedia notes that contouring products come as powder palettes and as cream products, with cream giving a more intense effect [3].

Westman Atelier's Face Trace Contour Stick launched in a single shade, Biscuit, and later added Truffle and Ganache; its full-size stick is $48 and a mini is $25, according to Refinery29. The same article lists budget alternatives including Milk Makeup's cream bronzer stick ($24), Makeup By Mario's SoftSculpt shaping stick ($30) and a Nudestix bronzer stick ($35) [1].

L'Oreal Paris advises applying cream or liquid foundation first, skipping powder under a cream contour, swiping the stick along the cheek hollows, jawline, sides of the nose and temples, then blending with a makeup blender and finishing with cream blush and setting spray. It suggests a shade one to two tones darker than the skin to avoid harsh contrast [2]. Westman Atelier founder Gucci Westman traces the stick where she wants shadow and blends upward with fingers or a brush [1].

Refinery29 reported that the Westman Atelier stick became a TikTok favourite as cream contour grew popular after Hailey Bieber's 'underpainting' video, and that makeup artist Mary Phillips, who works with Bieber, uses it [1]. Contouring itself dates to Elizabethan actors using chalk and soot, with film makeup artists such as Max Factor Sr. later using shading, Kevyn Aucoin popularising sculpted makeup in the 1990s and celebrities such as Kim Kardashian driving a surge in the 2010s [3].

A stick is a non-surgical option for people who want more visible bone structure in photos and is often paired with a brush or sponge for blending. It sits among other temporary appearance tools such as highlighter and bronzer.

L'Oreal Paris notes that contour products should not replace sunscreen, since they are not applied across the whole face [2]. Product labels generally advise patch testing for sensitive skin and removing makeup before sleep, and heavy cream formulas may suit some skin types more than others.

timeline.event: Elizabethan actors use chalk and soot to define faces on stage [3].
Kevyn Aucoin popularises sculpted makeup; his 2000 book brings it to the general public [3].
Celebrities such as Kim Kardashian drive a surge in contouring and brands launch contour and strobing products [3].
Westman Atelier's Face Trace Contour Stick is reported as a TikTok favourite [1].
